NAAVIK GAMING PODCAST
How Behavioral AI Helps Fight Cheating
By Devin Becker   •   October 6, 2026
As cheating becomes more sophisticated, anti-cheat is increasingly shifting from detecting software to understanding player behavior. Host
Devin Becker
is joined by
André Pimenta Ribeiro
, CEO & Co-Founder of Anybrain, to discuss how behavioral anti-cheat analyzes player inputs, where it fits alongside traditional tools, and why some approaches avoid software access entirely. The conversation explores the business impact of cheating on retention and revenue, when studios should begin investing in prevention, and how even smaller teams can approach the problem. André also breaks down the growing cheat-as-a-service economy, the challenge posed by AI and hardware-assisted cheats, the risks of false positives for legitimate players, and how behavioral data could expand beyond cheating detection over the next several years.

Hello everyone, I'm your host Devin Becker and today I'm delighted to be joined by André Pimenta Ribeiro, CEO and co-founder of Anybrain.
Anybrain is an AI anti-cheat platform that detects cheating by analyzing how players use their mouse, keyboard, controller, or touchscreen rather than just scanning game software. So today we're actually going to discuss how AI is changing both sides of the fight against cheating, both for the cheaters and for the anti-cheats. Hopefully more so for the latter, but we'll see.
But just to start things off, André, can you give us a quick overview of your background and how research on mental fatigue actually turned into an anti-cheat company?

Yeah, sure. Well, first of all, thank you very much for the, the invitation. So, I founded Anybrain almost 11 years ago.
I started doing a research on University of Minho, it's a local university, on looking for human-computer interaction and how we need to use some of our cognitive skills to, to u- use machines. On the time, we were developing an algorithm to detect mental fatigue, and it's how we started Anybrain.
So, I was doing my PhD on creating an algorithm that was able to detect how tired we, we are while using the computer. During that time, and s- we also learned that, okay, , it's ... When we are using the computer, it's not only ab- about being tired or how we perform it. We can use this information for more stuff.
But we decide to start the company then. We initially tried to explore the mental fatigue side on the beginning, not only on the gaming. We work with different, different industries where people were spending time on the computer. At the end, what we wanted is to give some advice like stop for five minutes or come back in a, in a few.
We were introduced to the gaming when we started working with esports organizations in 2019, selling same software, we had some requests on some performance coach. They were asking, "Hey, can you apply your tech for esports? Because it's hard to control the, the players or helping them to perform better."
We said yes, and that was the moment that, okay, we need to do this for gaming industry and not only about mental fatigue. This can also be related with cheating, about identity, because at the end, one thing that in the gaming it's unique, we need to interact with the games to be able to play. They were made on that way. So, let's explore the human-computer interaction field with AI. That was our expertise.
Devin:
Interesting. So definitely like on the behavioral side of things, looking at that, analyzing it, and then figuring out, hey, this actually helps us figure out if people are doing things maybe that, they normally wouldn't be doing that maybe the computer's doing for them or helping them.
So out of curiosity then, how does detecting cheats from like player inputs work, and how is that different from like a traditional anti-cheat?
André:
Yeah. So the, the main difference is that we look for, the behavior of the player and not for the machine itself. We are not looking for what kind of software you have installed, if there is something that is trying to access the, the memory of the game or trying to tampering with the files.
What we look is, okay, if someone is able to do it, because we know at some point, they will, we will understand if that behavior is possible or not, and how this behavior can translate in detecting these some kind of hacks, let's say. So, a- as I started presenting, uh, u- the human performance while using the computer is unique per player and it's also unique between humans and non-humans.
When, when I'm talking about non-humans, could be bots, could be a script for an aimbot, could be a, an advanced hack that is helping to aim, is helping to adjust, for example, the recoil or, is taking decisions, as we are seeing nowadays a lot of AI bots as well that can take decisions. They can move on levels more than a static software.
So, with this, we look, okay, let's say I will give the example of an aimbot that it's probably one of the most known hacks on, on gaming, mainly on FPS. We need to aim on opponent and the way we do it, if we do it faster, will be better for us because it will give us an advantage.
